title: The DOJ Just Threatened to Prosecute Election Officials Over Voter Rolls. Naturalized Indian Americans Could Pay the Price.
excerpt: Chandigarh-born Harmeet Dhillon sent criminal warnings to all 50 states. The database her department wants states to use has already flagged eligible citizens for removal.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • DOJ warns election officials of prosecution for retaining noncitizens on voter rolls.
  • Naturalized citizens, especially Indian Americans, risk wrongful removal due to outdated databases.
  • Conflicting court rulings create legal uncertainty over voter roll purges.
  • Indian Americans, a growing demographic, face challenges in maintaining voting rights.
  • Midterm elections heighten stakes for voter participation among Indian Americans.

The Department of Justice sent letters to election officials in all 50 states this week, warning them they could face criminal prosecution if they allow noncitizens to remain on voter rolls. The threat came from Harmeet Kaur Dhillon — born in Chandigarh, raised between London and North Carolina, and now the most powerful Indian American in American law enforcement as the Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights.

The irony is hard to miss. The very databases Dhillon's department wants states to use to purge their voter rolls have a documented history of wrongly flagging naturalized citizens — the same immigrant community Dhillon herself belongs to.

The Warning

In her letter, Dhillon put state election officials on notice with language that left little room for ambiguity. "Any election officer, including the chief election officer of the state, who knowingly retains noncitizens on the state's voter registration list or facilitates noncitizens in receiving and casting ballots could be subject to criminal liability," she wrote.

The letters are the latest escalation in the Trump administration's campaign to take greater federal control over elections, which the Constitution assigns to individual states. Since taking office, the DOJ's Civil Rights Division has sued 30 states and Washington, D.C., over their voter roll maintenance practices. Dhillon told the Daily Caller her division has found "hundreds, if not thousands" of dead people and noncitizens still registered to vote.

The department is also deploying election monitors to 12 jurisdictions ahead of upcoming primaries, including Maricopa County, Arizona; Detroit, Michigan; and Fairfax County, Virginia — areas with significant immigrant populations.

The Database Problem

At the center of this fight is a federal system called SAVE — Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements. Originally designed to help agencies verify immigration status for benefit applications, the Trump administration retooled it into a searchable national citizenship-tracking system by folding in Social Security records and other federal databases.

The problem: SAVE doesn't update in real time. When someone becomes a naturalized citizen, their records in the system may not reflect that change for months or even years. States that cross-reference their voter rolls against SAVE have already canceled the registrations of voters who were flagged as noncitizens — including people who had legally naturalized and were fully eligible to vote.

Voting-rights groups including the League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center have warned that the system "frequently flags eligible American citizens due to outdated government records, placing them at severe risk of immediate disenfranchisement."

> ""This case implicates two fundamental rights that protect Americans from government overreach: the right to privacy and the right to vote," Sooknanan wrote."

In Texas, when the state ran its 18 million registered voters through the expanded SAVE system last year, it flagged 2,724 as "potential noncitizens." Reporting by Votebeat later found that some of those flagged voters had already provided proof of citizenship through their state driver's license applications.

Two Courts, Two Orders, One Mess

The SAVE system is now trapped between contradictory federal court orders. On Monday, U.S. District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan in Washington, D.C. — a Biden appointee — ruled that the Trump administration violated the Social Security Act, the Privacy Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act when it overhauled the database. She blocked DHS from providing states access to the expanded system.

"This case implicates two fundamental rights that protect Americans from government overreach: the right to privacy and the right to vote," Sooknanan wrote. "The federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote."

But on the same day, a Florida judge went the other direction. U.S. District Judge Timothy Wetherell ordered DHS to give four states — including Florida — access to citizenship data for voter checks, directly contradicting Sooknanan's ruling.

"The court understands that this puts defendants in a bind because they are subject to two contradictory orders," Wetherell acknowledged. "One of the orders has to give."

The conflict will likely be resolved by federal appeals courts, but in the meantime, states are operating in legal limbo — some purging voters based on SAVE data, others blocked from accessing it.

What This Means for Indian Americans

Indian Americans are the second-fastest-growing immigrant group in the United States, with an estimated 4.8 million people of Indian origin living in the country. Of those, roughly 2.6 million are naturalized citizens — people who went through the legal process, passed the civics test, took the oath, and earned the right to vote.

They are precisely the population most vulnerable to SAVE's known flaws. Someone who entered the U.S. on an H-1B visa, spent years in the green card backlog, and finally naturalized may still appear as a noncitizen in federal databases that haven't caught up. If their state runs a SAVE check and their record is outdated, they could be flagged for removal from the voter rolls — and now, under Dhillon's new guidance, the election official who doesn't remove them could face prosecution.

The chilling effect is the quiet part. Even if wrongly flagged voters can contest their removal, the burden falls on them to prove their own citizenship to participate in the democracy they legally joined. For an immigrant community that already navigated one of the world's most arduous immigration systems to earn that right, the additional obstacle stings.

"States are not doing their job to remove people from the voter rolls," Dhillon told the Daily Caller. But voting-rights advocates argue that the bigger threat to election integrity isn't the vanishingly small number of noncitizens who vote — multiple studies have confirmed it's statistically negligible — but the systematic removal of eligible voters who happen to share demographic characteristics with recent immigrants.

The Midterm Stakes

The timing matters. November's midterm elections will decide control of Congress, and Indian American voter participation has surged in recent cycles. In the 2024 presidential election, Indian Americans voted at higher rates than the general population, and both parties have been aggressively courting the community.

The DOJ's courtroom record on this front has been mixed. Federal judges have blocked Trump's executive orders requiring proof of citizenship to register to vote and restricting mail-in ballots. The First Circuit recently declined to fast-track the DOJ's appeals of those rulings, denying the administration's preferred timeline.

But the political pressure campaign — threatening prosecution of election officials who don't purge aggressively enough — may accomplish through intimidation what the courts have denied through litigation. Officials who fear criminal liability may err on the side of over-purging, removing eligible voters rather than risk prosecution for keeping a questionable registration active.

For the 2.6 million naturalized Indian Americans whose citizenship is a matter of public record but whose SAVE data may tell a different story, the message is clear: check your voter registration. Do it now, and do it again before November.

*Sources: Reuters, CNN, Daily Caller, NBC Palm Springs, Washington Examiner, Votebeat, Democracy Docket*
